findings.committee: Greater Manchester Combined Authority
findings.headline: PWLB 10-year rates at 5.72% on 31 March 2026, up sharply after Middle East conflict
findings.detail: PWLB rates were volatile through 2025/26. Ten-year gilt yields fell to around 4.23% in late February 2026 before spiking upward. By 31 March 2026, the 10-year PWLB Certainty rate had risen to 5.72% and the 25-year rate to 6.29%, with the 25-year having reached 6.43% intraday in late March. The paper attributes this to "inflation concerns emanating from the on-going conflict in the Middle East" and "steepening energy costs."
findings.matters: The sharp March rise in long-term rates materially increases the cost of converting temporary funding to permanent debt. This shift occurred after the authority deferred long-term borrowing, making future refinancing of the £100m temporary borrowing (maturing April 2026) more expensive.
findings.figures: 10-year PWLB: low 5.13% (02 March 2026), high 5.88% (27 March 2026), closed 5.72%; 25-year: low 5.78%, high 6.43% (27 March 2026), closed 6.29%; 1-year closed 5.04%
findings.quote: At the close of 31 March 2026, the 1-year PWLB Certainty rate was 5.04% whilst the 5-, 10-, 25-and 50-year rates were 5.28%, 5.72%, 6.29% and 6.08% respectively.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Combined Authority
findings.headline: Under-borrowed position increased to £1,138.8m; CFR not fully funded by debt
findings.detail: The Capital Financing Requirement rose to £2,506.017m but the authority's gross borrowing position was £1,367.187m, leaving an under-borrowed position of £1,138.830m (up from £1,056.143m in 2024/25). The £82.7m increase in under-borrowing means the authority is relying on cash and reserves to cover the gap. The authority states this was "prudent" because "near-term investment rates have generally been lower than medium to long-term borrowing costs."
findings.matters: An increasing under-borrowed position of £1.1bn indicates growing reliance on reserves and liquid investments to fund net capital need. Risk arises if: (a) investment yields fall below borrowing costs, (b) unexpected cash demands require asset sales, or (c) interest rates rise unexpectedly.
findings.figures: CFR £2,506.017m; gross borrowing position £1,367.187m; under-borrowed £1,138.830m (up from £1,056.143m); increase of £82.7m
findings.quote: During 2025/26, the Authority maintained an under-borrowed position. This meant that the capital borrowing need, (the CFR), was not fully funded with loan debt as cash supporting the Authority's reserves, balances and cash flow was used as an interim measure.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Combined Authority
findings.headline: No long-term borrowing undertaken; £100m temporary borrowing at 4.90–5.30% instead
findings.detail: Despite capital expenditure of £520.2m and unfinanced requirement of £107.9m, the authority made no long-term borrowing during 2025/26. Instead it undertook £100m of temporary borrowing from other councils and funds (Pension Protection Fund £20m, London Treasury Liquidity Fund £50m, and four local authorities) at rates of 4.90–5.30%, maturing in April 2026. The authority cites "elevated cost of borrowing" for deferring long-term funding.
findings.matters: Deferring long-term borrowing signals expectation that PWLB rates will fall, reducing near-term costs but deferring refinancing risk and depending on continued access to temporary funding markets.
findings.figures: Temporary borrowing £100m at 4.90–5.30%; 10-year PWLB average for year 5.38%; no long-term borrowing undertaken
findings.quote: Due to the elevated cost of borrowing, no long-term borrowing was undertaken during the year.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Combined Authority
findings.headline: Gross borrowing reduced by £74m; average cost fell from 3.78% to 3.58%
findings.detail: Total external borrowings fell from £1,417.353m to £1,343.241m (£74m reduction), reflecting active debt management and maturing debt not being refinanced. Average cost of borrowing improved from 3.78% to 3.58% through a combination of repayments and refinancing at lower rates. PWLB debt fell from £476.019m to £452.117m; market debt from £813.302m to £778.089m.
findings.matters: Debt reduction and cost improvement reduce future interest charges. However this must be assessed against the increased under-borrowed position, which creates dependency on maintaining adequate reserve levels.
findings.figures: Total external borrowings £1,343.241m (down £74.112m from £1,417.353m); average rate 3.58% (down from 3.78%); PWLB £452.117m (down £23.9m); market £778.089m (down £35.2m)
findings.quote: Total external borrowings 1,417.353 ... 1,343.241

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Combined Authority
findings.headline: Earmarked reserves reduced by £53.3m to £462.6m
findings.detail: Earmarked reserves fell from £515.931m to £462.626m, a drawdown of £53.305m. Total usable resources (balances, reserves, receipts and provisions) declined from £773.578m to £715.640m. General balances were maintained at £44.944m. These reserves funded the authority's under-borrowed position where capital financing need was not fully covered by external debt.
findings.matters: A £53m reduction in earmarked reserves requires scrutiny of what is driving these drawdowns and whether remaining reserve balances remain adequate for known liabilities and contingencies.
findings.figures: Earmarked reserves £462.626m (down £53.305m from £515.931m); usable resources £715.640m (down £57.938m); general balances £44.944m (unchanged)
findings.quote: Earmarked reserves 515.931 462.626

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Combined Authority
findings.headline: Investment income £17.2m: 7.5× budget of £2.3m
findings.detail: The authority achieved investment income of £17.2m during 2025/26 against a budget of £2.3m, an outperformance of £14.9m. This was driven by maintaining an average balance of £410.6m of internally managed funds earning 4.19%, outperforming the SONIA benchmark of 4.01% by 18 basis points.
findings.matters: A £14.9m positive variance materially improves overall financial position. This out-performance reflects effective treasury management but is dependent on current high interest rates which are now falling.
findings.figures: Actual £17.2m vs budget £2.3m (variance £14.9m); average balance £410.6m; average return 4.19% vs SONIA 4.01% (18bps outperformance)
findings.quote: Total investment income was £17.2m compared to a budget of £2.3m.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Combined Authority
findings.headline: Capital expenditure £520.2m: £116m below budget
findings.detail: The authority spent £520.198m on capital expenditure against a budget of £636.317m, a shortfall of £116.119m. Unfinanced capital expenditure was £107.862m versus a budgeted £126.646m. This follows 2024/25 when actual capital spend was £624.795m, indicating two consecutive years of capital underspend relative to budget.
findings.matters: Significant capital underspend raises questions about delivery capacity, project slippage or reprioritisation — critical for lenders assessing a council's ability to execute its capital programme and manage borrowing need.
findings.figures: 2025/26 actual £520.198m vs budget £636.317m (underspend £116.119m); unfinanced £107.862m vs budget £126.646m; 2024/25 actual £624.795m

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Combined Authority
findings.headline: Waste and Resources creating new Emissions Trading Scheme Reserve (£5.0m) to prepare for future carbon emissions cost liability when energy-from-waste facilities enter ETS scheme.
findings.detail: New Emissions Trading Scheme Reserve established at £5.0m to smooth levy for expected cost increases when carbon emissions from energy-from-waste facilities are included in the ETS. Implementation date subject to Government confirmation. Proactive reserve building signals future cost liability is anticipated but timeline remains uncertain.
findings.matters: Authority preparing for known regulatory change that will impose new carbon costs on waste treatment; future waste levies will face material cost pressures from ETS pricing when it takes effect.
findings.figures: New ETS Reserve £5.0m (31 Mar 2026)
findings.quote: The Emissions Trading Scheme Reserve has been created to help smooth the levy for expected increases when the carbon emissions from energy from waste (EfW) facilities are included in the Emissions Trading Scheme (implementation date subject to confirmation from Government).

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Combined Authority
findings.headline: GMFRS reserves increased from £44.618m to £47.659m through transfers for revenue-funded capital projects and digital transformation.
findings.detail: GMFRS built reserves through transfers totaling £4.821m, including £2.498m commitment for revenue-funded capital projects (where GMFRS receives no specific capital funding), £1.311m for digital transformation of prevention and protection services, and £0.460m of Local Remediation Action Plan grant. Partially offset increased insurance provision (£1.479m) and insurance reserve release (£0.872m).
findings.matters: Fire service funding its own capital projects and strategic transformation through revenue reserves indicates limited capital funding from central sources; reserve level demonstrates fiscal conservatism but signals capital funding constraint.
findings.figures: GMFRS total reserves £44.618m (1 Apr 2025) to £47.659m (31 Mar 2026); net reserve transfer in £3.041m
findings.quote: Transfers to reserves totalled £4.821m which includes a £2.498m commitment for revenue funded capital projects for which GMFRS receive no specific funding, £1.311m for future investment into the prevention and protection digital transformation project and £0.460m of Local Remediation Action Plan grant for future spend.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Combined Authority
findings.headline: GMFRS fire estate requires ongoing investment due to repairs and maintenance cost pressures across stations and specialist facilities.
findings.detail: GMFRS premises costs overran by £0.901m due to repairs and maintenance pressures across estate including stations, Bury Training & Safety Centre, Leigh Technical Services Centre and headquarters. Overspend within £5.771m revised budget signals aging facility challenges and ongoing capital investment requirements.
findings.matters: Fire service facility condition is critical to operational readiness and safety; ongoing maintenance pressures indicate either deferred maintenance accumulation or aging assets, informing lenders' assessment of long-term capital requirements.
findings.figures: GMFRS premises costs £6.671m vs revised budget £5.771m; overspend £0.901m
findings.quote: Premises costs have overspent by £0.901m in 2025/26 which is mainly due to repairs and maintenance pressures across the GMFRS estate which includes Stations, Bury Training & Safety Centre, Leigh Technical Services Centre and GMFRS Headquarters

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Combined Authority
findings.headline: Digital programme slippage of £0.692m expected to be spent in 2026/27, mainly within the GM One Network programme.
findings.detail: Digital services experienced £1.092m total reduction vs Q3 forecast: £0.4m reduction in Digital Strategy expenditure due to delays in AI-related work (mainly Central Government funding announcement delays), and £0.692m programme slippage in GM One Network expected to be spent in 2026/27. Indicates delivery challenges or resource constraints.
findings.matters: Programme slippage moves committed resources into future years; signals whether GM One Network and Digital Strategy are progressing to schedule or facing delivery complexity.
findings.figures: Digital expenditure £5.504m vs Q3 forecast £6.596m; reduction £1.092m; programme slippage £0.692m
findings.quote: £0.692m relating to digital programme slippage that is expected to be spent in 2026/27, mainly within the GM One Network programme.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Combined Authority
findings.headline: Education Work and Skills expenditure underperformed by £9.661m due to payment-by-results contract performance and accounting treatment changes in Integrated Settlement.
findings.detail: Education Work & Skills underspent £9.661m: £6.0m from lower than forecast payment-by-results contract performance across procured and level 3 learning providers; £3.0m from change in accounting treatment of Integrated Settlement underspend (now receipt in advance per grant conditions); £0.661m other underspends to be carried forward to 2026/27. Payment-by-results underspend suggests lower service delivery or outcomes achieved.
findings.matters: £9.661m variance in major service area (£121.461m original budget) is significant; £6.0m payment-by-results underspend indicates lower delivery or demand, raising questions about whether this is structural or temporary.
findings.figures: Education Work & Skills expenditure £140.911m vs Q3 forecast £150.572m; variance £9.661m (payment-by-results £6.0m, accounting treatment £3.0m)
findings.quote: At outturn, Education, Work & Skills expenditure was £140.911m which represents a reduction in expenditure of £9.661m due to: £6.000m reduction in Adult Skills delivery relating to payment by results contracts across the procured and level 3 learning providers.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Combined Authority
findings.headline: Ring and Ride (Accessible Transport) costs rising due to inflation and employment cost pressures, with operational model review underway to optimize service delivery.
findings.detail: Accessible Transport (door-to-door minibus service for older and disabled people) costs rising due to inflationary pressures, employment costs, vehicle and depot lease costs. TfGM commissioned Neighbourhood Transport Review to identify optimal commercial and operating model for Ring and Ride and Local Link integration with Bee Network, indicating recognition of sustainability challenges.
findings.matters: Demand-led service serving growing elderly demographic faces mounting cost pressures; management review signals recognition of current model unsustainability, with potential for service changes or charging modifications that may face political resistance.
findings.figures: Ring and Ride costs increased c.£1m in Q2 outturn; budget unchanged since Q3 reforecast at £4.730m; capital commitment for service
findings.quote: The additional costs are primarily due to rising inflationary costs and increases related to employment costs, vehicle and depot lease costs and other general inflation. TfGM are carrying out the Neighbourhood Transport Review which is looking at the most optimal commercial and operating model going forward for Ring and Ride

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Combined Authority
findings.headline: GM Fire & Rescue overtime spending reduced by £1.4m compared to 2024/25 following management review commenced August 2025.
findings.detail: Following a review of overtime led by the Chief Fire Officer commenced August 2025, overtime spend in 2025/26 was £1.957m compared to £2.4m in 2024/25, a reduction of £1.4m. Demonstrates active management intervention in controllable costs within a personnel-heavy budget.
findings.matters: Shows operational management engaging actively to control non-essential expenditure; indicates cost discipline, though sustainability depends on whether controls can be maintained long-term.
findings.figures: Overtime 2025/26 £1.957m vs 2024/25 £2.4m; reduction of £1.4m
findings.quote: In August 2025, a review commenced with a focus on overtime led by the Chief Fire Officer. The impact of this action has impacted actual overtime paid and has resulted in a £1.4m reduction in the expenditure compared to 2024/25.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Combined Authority
findings.headline: Transport fuel costs increased following geopolitical shock (Iran War starting February) feeding through franchised bus operator payments linked to diesel prices.
findings.detail: Bus franchising net operating costs outturned £2.3m above budget due to fuel price impacts from Iran War commencing February 2026, feeding through to payments to franchised operators whose costs are partially linked to diesel market price. Partially offset by strong patronage and revenue growth in Tranche 1 and 2.
findings.matters: Demonstrates exposure to external geopolitical shocks in contracted service delivery; lenders need to assess whether hedging or contractual protections exist for fuel price volatility.
findings.figures: Bus franchising net cost £228.692m vs Q3 forecast £227.573m (variance £1.119m reflected in summary); additional fuel cost impact c.£2.3m above budget
findings.quote: The Iran War started to impact fuel prices from early February and this subsequently feeds through into the payments to franchised operators which are partially linked to the market price for diesel.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Combined Authority
findings.headline: Waste operational costs swung £15.7m due to market-driven factors including recyclate revenues, waste volumes and landfill costs.
findings.detail: Waste operational cost variance of £15.7m driven by changes in waste volumes and market prices. Recyclate revenue rebate provided £3.0m benefit, residual value contract benefits £5.4m, offset partly by landfill cost increases (£2.0m overspend). Demonstrates significant external cost exposure within a service area where input costs are largely externally determined.
findings.matters: Large volatility in a major service area shows commodity market exposure; lenders need to assess whether reserves and margins adequately buffer these swings.
findings.figures: Operational cost variance £15.7m: Recyclate revenue rebate £3.0m benefit; Residual value contract (including third-party income) £5.4m benefit; Landfill £2.0m overspend
findings.quote: The Operational Costs variance from budget has been driven by changes in waste volumes and market costs.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Combined Authority
findings.headline: Waste and Resources planned Insurance Reserve draw-down support, used to smooth the levy due to high inflation, ends in 2026/27.
findings.detail: A planned £4m transfer from Insurance Reserve smoothed the waste levy in 2025/26 following high inflation years. This annual support mechanism ends in 2026/27, creating forward budget pressure unless alternative funding solutions are identified. Total Waste earmarked reserves declining from £69.7m to £59.0m.
findings.matters: A known funding pressure point for 2026/27 signals the authority will need to increase the levy on constituent councils or identify cost reductions, both of which require stakeholder negotiation.
findings.figures: Insurance Reserve transfer £4.0m in 2025/26 is last year of planned support; total Waste earmarked reserves £69.7m (31 Mar 2025) declining to £59.0m (31 Mar 2026)
findings.quote: The transfer of £4m from the Insurance Reserve was budgeted for and used to smooth the levy from previous years high inflation. 2026/27 is the last year of that planned support.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Combined Authority
findings.headline: All GMCA budget areas achieved breakeven position for 2025/26 after transfers to and from earmarked reserves.
findings.detail: The GMCA General Budget, Mayoral General Budget, GM Fire & Rescue, Waste and Resources, and Transport (including TfGM) all reported breakeven revenue outturn positions for 2025/26, achieved through management of variances across individual service areas and strategic use of reserve transfers.
findings.matters: Demonstrates financial control across multi-service operations, though reliance on reserve transfers to achieve breakeven signals potential sustainability risks ahead.
findings.figures: All five budget areas: Net position £0m
findings.quote: The GMCA General Budget revenue outturn position for 2025/26 is breakeven after transfers to/from earmarked reserves.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Combined Authority
findings.paper_title: 6 GMCA Report Group Interim CEO Sept 2026 v2
findings.headline: Interim Group Chief Executive appointed at salary of £262k, above the previously approved range of £220k–£250k.
findings.detail: Andrew Lightfoot is appointed as Interim Group Chief Executive from 28 August 2026. His salary of £262k exceeds the previously approved range due to pay awards applied in the intervening period. The costs will be met from existing senior leadership budgets, creating no new budget pressure.
findings.matters: Finance directors track senior leadership cost commitments and budget adherence; a salary above an approved range raises questions about approval processes and budget control.
findings.figures: £262k versus £220k–£250k (previously approved range)
findings.quote: The Combined Authority has previously approved the renumeration for the role at a range between £220k to £250k. The remuneration is currently at £262k, given the ensuing pay awards in the intervening period.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Combined Authority
findings.headline: Declarations of interest process improved after previous No Assurance audit opinion but further work needed to fully embed controls
findings.detail: Progress was noted in relation to declarations of interest arrangements following a previous No Assurance audit opinion. Improvements have been made to strengthen the process, increase completion rates and provide greater visibility of officer declarations. However, it was acknowledged that work was needed to streamline the approach to maintain appropriate transparency, accountability and audit assurance. The Committee emphasised the importance of continuing to monitor to ensure processes are embedded effectively.
findings.matters: Governance failures in declarations and conflicts of interest are control weaknesses that can enable fraud or poor decision-making. Previous No Assurance rating indicates a serious prior control failure; remediation progress is positive but incomplete embedding remains a risk.
findings.figures: Previous audit opinion: No Assurance; current status: improved but requiring further streamlining
findings.quote: It was noted that improvements had been made to strengthen the process, increase completion rates and provide greater visibility of officer declarations. The Committee was advised that the declarations process also supported the preparation of the Statement of Accounts, however it was acknowledged that work was needed to be done to streamline the approach to maintain appropriate transparency, accountability and audit assurance.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Combined Authority
findings.headline: Significant number of overdue ICT-related audit actions remain outstanding, raising cyber resilience concerns
findings.detail: A number of overdue ICT related actions remain outstanding. Members expressed concern regarding the volume of ICT actions outstanding and potential implications for cyber resilience and organisational assurance. A deep-dive session on ICT has been scheduled for September. A new Group Chief Digital and Information Officer is taking up post in August and will engage with the Committee regarding ICT governance, cyber security and digital transformation.
findings.matters: Cybersecurity is a material operational and financial risk for any organisation. Outstanding audit actions suggest weaknesses in IT controls that could impact data security, operational resilience and expose the organisation to financial loss.
findings.figures: Multiple overdue ICT-related actions remain outstanding
findings.quote: Members expressed concern regarding the volume of ICT actions outstanding and the potential implications for cyber resilience and organisational assurance.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Combined Authority
findings.headline: Going Concern Assessment confirms GMCA remains a going concern with balanced budget, strong reserves and multi-year funding certainty
findings.detail: The Going Concern Assessment supporting the draft accounts concludes GMCA remained a going concern, supported by a balanced approved budget, strong reserve levels, multi-year funding certainty through the Integrated Settlement, and robust financial planning arrangements. The Committee noted the robustness of the assessment including consideration of financial performance, reserves, liquidity and treasury management.
findings.matters: A lender requires assurance that the borrower can meet its obligations and sustain operations. This confirms the fundamental financial resilience position.
findings.figures: Balanced approved budget; strong reserve levels; multi-year funding certainty through Integrated Settlement
findings.quote: the assessment concluded GMCA remained a going concern, supported by: • A balanced approved budget. • Strong reserve levels. • Multi-year funding certainty through the Integrated Settlement. • Robust financial planning arrangements.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Combined Authority
findings.headline: Internal Audit opinion remains Reasonable Assurance but declining implementation performance risks weakening control environment
findings.detail: Overall internal audit opinion of Reasonable Assurance has been provided, consistent with the previous year. Concern was expressed regarding declining implementation performance where agreed actions remain outstanding beyond target dates. This could weaken the overall control environment and limit the level of assurance that could be provided. It was agreed to raise this with senior leadership.
findings.matters: Declining implementation of audit recommendations signals that management is not embedding audit findings. This allows control weaknesses to persist and is a red flag for financial control quality.
findings.figures: Reasonable Assurance opinion; action implementation rates fallen below target
findings.quote: Concern was expressed regarding declining implementation performance, particularly where agreed actions remained outstanding beyond target dates, as this could weaken the overall control environment and limit the level of assurance that could be provided.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Combined Authority
findings.headline: Draft accounts produced within statutory deadlines while GMCA moves through phased multi-year recovery toward unqualified audit opinion
findings.detail: Draft accounts for 2025/26 were produced within statutory deadlines and authorised for issue on 10 July 2026 following previous years' disclaimed audit opinions. The authority is expected to move through a phased recovery process over the next two years before returning to an unqualified audit opinion. Significant progress has been made in improving financial reporting arrangements, particularly within TfGM, but successful completion of the TfGM accounts rebuild remains a critical dependency.
findings.matters: A lender needs visibility of audit qualification recovery trajectory and timeline. Multi-year phased recovery indicates ongoing weaknesses in financial reporting systems that will require sustained management attention.
findings.figures: Draft accounts authorised for issue 10 July 2026; phased recovery expected to take two years
findings.quote: Whilst significant progress has been made in producing the 2025/26 draft accounts, GMCA is expected to move through a phased recovery process over the next two years before returning to an unqualified audit opinion, with successful completion of the TfGM accounts rebuild remaining a critical dependency.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Combined Authority
findings.headline: Transport grant funding drawn at £74.0m against budget of £141.9m, with major grant-funded programmes underspent.
findings.detail: Transport funding shows grants budgeted at £141.9m but only £74.0m drawn. The shortfall of £67.9m reflects underspend across grant-funded schemes including Active Travel (£3.3m underspend), Rapid Transit (£0.2m), and rephasing of local authority highways schemes.
findings.matters: Significant underutilisation of allocated grant funding can result in clawback or loss of future grant entitlement. Indicates the authority did not deploy available external grant funding at planned rates, affecting the authority's track record with government funders.
findings.figures: Transport grants: £74.0m drawn vs £141.9m budgeted; shortfall £67.9m
findings.quote: Transport ... Grants 141,931 [budget] 74,036 [outturn]

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Combined Authority
findings.headline: Major waste infrastructure schemes delayed: Household Waste Recycling Centre (Manchester) and Materials Recovery Facility (Bolton).
findings.detail: Waste Operational Assets outturn of £19.4m against forecast of £31.6m. Paper identifies delays in delivery of new Household Waste Recycling Centre (Manchester) and new Materials Recovery Facility (Bolton), alongside rephasing of fire suppression schemes.
findings.matters: Delays to major waste infrastructure affect operational resilience and capacity for future years. Given government focus on waste infrastructure, slippage on these schemes signals broader delivery challenges in the authority's capital programmes.
findings.figures: £19.4m outturn vs £31.6m forecast; underspend £12.2m
findings.quote: The total 2025/26 expenditure is £19.4m, this is a reduction of £12.2m since the last forecast due to reprofiling of fire suppression and detection schemes to 2026/27 and delays in the delivery of two large capital schemes, a new Household Waste Recycling Centre in Manchester and a new Materials Recovery Facility in Bolton.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Combined Authority
findings.headline: Bus Depots and Zero Emission Buses programme overspent by £4.1m with Oldham and Hyde Road phase 2 accelerating ahead of plan.
findings.detail: Bus Depots & ZEB recorded expenditure of £60.1m against forecast of £56.0m. Oldham and Hyde Road phase 2 electrification started earlier than anticipated and progressed ahead of forecast. This is one of few schemes where actual spend exceeded forecast.
findings.matters: In a capital programme dominated by rephasing delays, acceleration on a core electrification scheme demonstrates delivery capability and suggests bus franchising infrastructure is progressing, though it has consumed budget forecast for later years.
findings.figures: £60.1m outturn vs £56.0m forecast; overspend £4.1m
findings.quote: The total expenditure for 2025/26 was £60.1m, compared to a previous forecast of £56.0m. This is due to Oldham and Hyde Road phase 2 electrification starting earlier than anticipated and progressing ahead of forecast.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Combined Authority
findings.headline: Brownfield Land Fund rephased by £38.7m due to development complexity and delays.
findings.detail: Brownfield Land Fund recorded expenditure of £25.3m against forecast of £64.0m. Underspend attributed to "complex nature of development causing delays" with expenditure reprofiled into later years. Scheme is funded from central government's Integrated Settlement.
findings.matters: A £38.7m rephasing of grant-funded brownfield development signals delivery challenges in converting grant funding to housing outcomes. Creates risk of grant clawback or loss of future grant entitlement if deadlines slip further.
findings.figures: £25.3m outturn vs £64.0m forecast; underspend £38.7m
findings.quote: The total forecast for 2025/26 has decreased to £25.3m, as previously forecast expenditure has been re-profiled into later years, as a result of the complex nature of development causing delays.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Combined Authority
findings.headline: Warm Homes grant programmes significantly underspent with funding agreements and contracts signed after year-end.
findings.detail: Warm Homes: Social Housing Fund spent £0.5m against a quarter 3 forecast of £16.6m; Funding Agreements signed March–April 2026. Warm Homes: Local Grant spent £0.2m against quarter 3 forecast of £5.2m; contracts signed May–June 2026. Both described as in mobilisation phase, implying limited delivery before grant agreements in place.
findings.matters: Central government grant programmes with late-signed agreements risk clawback if end-of-year or multi-year deadlines slip. The scale of underspend (£21.2m combined) signals mobilisation risk on schemes intended to support vulnerable households.
findings.figures: Social Housing: £0.5m vs £16.6m forecast (underspend £16.1m); Local Grant: £0.2m vs £5.2m forecast (underspend £5.0m)
findings.quote: Grant Funding Agreements with registered social housing providers were signed in March and April 2026... Contracts were signed with the contractors in May & June 2026, which will enable to scale up the programme in 2026/27.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Combined Authority
findings.headline: Bus Shelter estate of 3,534 shelters moved from capital to revenue funding following March 2025 purchase.
findings.detail: The Bus Shelter estate was purchased in March 2025 but the authority now funds renewal from revenue budgets rather than capital. Recorded nil capital expenditure in 2025/26 against a previous forecast of £1.0m. This shifts funding source and creates a revenue budget pressure in future years.
findings.matters: A significant asset moving from capital to revenue funding increases operating budget pressure and affects capital efficiency metrics. Other councils managing comparable assets monitor such reclassifications.
findings.figures: £1.0m previously forecast, £0 outturn; 3,534 shelters in estate
findings.quote: The Bus Shelter estate, consisting of 3,534 shelters, was purchased in March 2025. The total expenditure for 2025/26 was nil, compared to the previous forecast of £1.0m. This is now being funded by revenue budgets.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Combined Authority
findings.headline: Capital programme outturn of £497.6m was £88.2m (15 per cent) below forecast, predominantly rephased delivery rather than savings.
findings.detail: Actual capital expenditure was £497.6m compared to a forecast of £585.9m in February 2026. The paper identifies most variance as rephasing of works into 2026/27 and beyond rather than permanent reductions. Major rephasing occurred across Brownfield Land Fund (£38.7m), Warm Homes programmes (£21.2m combined), Bury Interchange, Park & Ride, and various local authority schemes.
findings.matters: A 15% shortfall in a capital programme, even if rephased, indicates delivery challenges affecting long-term asset investment timelines and grant drawdown schedules. Finance directors in other authorities and lenders assess whether rephasing becomes serial slippage.
findings.figures: Actual expenditure £497.6m vs forecast £585.9m; variance £88.2m
findings.quote: The actual expenditure for 2025/26 was £497.6m, compared to a forecast for 2025/26 presented to GMCA 13 February 2026 of £585.9m.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Waste & Recycling Committee
findings.headline: Slower capital programme generated £3.6m financing benefit from reduced borrowing need and lower internal borrowing charges
findings.detail: Capital underspend of £9.7m (outturn £19.5m vs budget £29.2m) resulted in lower borrowing requirement. Authority benefited from £3.6m variance in operational financing from rebate of internal borrowing charges and reduced interest payable costs. Benefit is temporary pending progression of delayed major projects.
findings.matters: Lenders monitor borrowing trends and debt servicing costs; capital underspend provides short-term treasury benefit, though delayed projects must eventually progress and require funding
findings.figures: Capital variance £9.7m (outturn £19.5m vs budget £29.2m); operational financing variance £3.6m from lower internal borrowing charges
findings.quote: The variance of £3.6m has arisen due to a rebate of charges for internal borrowing and slower than expected capital expenditure reducing the need for borrowing and interest payable costs.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Waste & Recycling Committee
findings.headline: Emissions Trading Scheme reserve of £5.0m created to smooth future levy impact from EfW facility emissions inclusion in UK ETS
findings.detail: New earmarked reserve established in 2025/26 to address anticipated cost increases when energy-from-waste facility carbon emissions brought into the Emissions Trading Scheme. Implementation date subject to government confirmation. Reserve designed to smooth levy impact on districts.
findings.matters: Forward-looking policy risk shows authority anticipating material future cost increase from environmental policy; relevant to medium-term budget planning and future levy pressures on districts
findings.figures: ETS reserve £5.0m
findings.quote: The Emissions Trading Scheme Reserve has been created to help smooth the levy for expected increases when the carbon emissions from energy from waste (EfW) facilities are included in the Emissions Trading Scheme (implementation date subject to confirmation from Government).

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Waste & Recycling Committee
findings.headline: Operational cost underspend of £15.7m driven by changes in waste volumes and market-determined treatment costs
findings.detail: Variance across three contracts from movements in market prices and waste volumes. Key drivers: residual waste contract savings £5.4m (third-party income), recyclate revenue rebate £3.0m, landfill efficiency £2.4m, lifecycle variations £2.1m, partly offset by residual waste treatment overspend £2.0m. Reflects market volatility.
findings.matters: Finance directors need to understand stability of operational costs; high market volatility creates forecasting difficulty and can mask underlying cost control or structural pressures
findings.figures: Total variance £15.7m; residual value £5.4m; recyclate rebate £3.0m; landfill £2.4m; lifecycle £2.1m; residual waste treatment £2.0m overspend
findings.quote: The variance has been driven by changes in waste volumes and market costs.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Waste & Recycling Committee
findings.headline: Reliance Street HWRC delayed by unforeseen ground conditions; Salford Road MRF procurement paused pending planning; both reprofiled to future years
findings.detail: Two major capital projects delayed. Reliance Street experienced ground condition issues requiring programme delay and capital reprofiling. Salford Road MRF procurement temporarily paused by planning requirements, also reprofiled to future years. Both moved budgets forward.
findings.matters: Infrastructure delays affect service capacity and delivery; finance directors monitor capital execution and forward borrowing implications of reprofiled schemes
findings.figures: Reliance Street budget £4.5m, outturn £1.5m (£3.0m reprofiled); Salford Road budget £5.0m, outturn £nil (£5.0m reprofiled)
findings.quote: As reported elsewhere on the agenda the Reliance St HWRC project has experienced programme delay to unforeseen ground conditions. This has resulted in reprofiling of the capital budget to cater for the delay to the programme.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Waste & Recycling Committee
findings.headline: Over Hulton MRF requires rear building extension to mitigate noise concerns from nearby residential development, necessitating capital budget increase.
findings.detail: Planning permission was recently granted for a 60-home residential development located within 200m of the proposed MRF site. Bolton Council raised concerns about noise impacts on residents using garden areas. Noise modelling indicated external glass handling could generate high noise levels. The agreed mitigation is a rear building extension (20m x 25m) to bring glass handling operations indoors, assessed as feasible following consultation with Suez on operational and transport impacts.
findings.matters: This design change increases project capital cost (amount not yet quantified) as a result of planning mitigation requirements; it demonstrates how land use decisions affecting adjacent sites can materially alter project scope and cost.
findings.figures: 20m x 25m building extension required, 200m proximity of new residential development, 60 new homes
findings.quote: The building extension will require an increase in the capital budget for the project and further details will be considered at the 28t September meeting of GMCA.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Waste & Recycling Committee
findings.headline: Over Hulton MRF completion date moved to summer 2028, over one year later than previously forecast.
findings.detail: Planning application submitted in January 2026 has faced extended determination due to concerns about environmental, traffic and noise impacts. Stage 3 procurement was paused for six months from July while design options were reviewed. Preferred supplier appointment is now forecast for January 2027, subject to planning approval and procurement requirements.
findings.matters: Significant programme delay of over one year affects forecast service delivery and extends capital spend profile; finance directors and lenders need to understand revised investment timescale and cash flow implications.
findings.figures: Completion moved to summer 2028, planning application submitted January 2026, 6-month procurement pause from July 2026, preferred supplier appointment forecast January 2027
findings.quote: As a result of these delays, overall project completion is now expected to move back to summer 2028.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Waste & Recycling Committee
findings.headline: Northern slope retaining wall solution provisionally costed at £700k with 15-week programme, the largest single cost item in the Reliance Street overrun.
findings.detail: Ground investigation revealed the northern slope adjacent to Moston Brook does not meet current geotechnical standards and is at risk of settlement due to steep gradient and poor-quality made ground. The provisional solution comprises 75 concrete piles installed to 18 metres depth with steel anchor ties and concrete capping beam. The design is under review to determine whether pile numbers can be reduced. This is expected to result in substantial additional cost and programme delays, including possible temporary site shutdown.
findings.matters: The slope mitigation is the largest remaining cost unknown and the primary driver of further programme delays; it represents the highest outstanding risk to both project cost and timeline to service reopening.
findings.figures: £700k provisional estimate, £150k miscellaneous costs, 75 concrete piles, 18 metre depth, 15-week installation programme
findings.quote: A slope stability risk assessment found that the northern slope is at risk of settlement due to its steep gradient and poor-quality made ground. A retaining solution is therefore required to stabilise the slope and surrounding ground. A provisional solution proposes a piled retaining wall along the northern boundary, comprising 75 concrete piles installed to a depth of 18 metres.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Waste & Recycling Committee
findings.headline: Reliance Street HWRC capital budget forecast at £5.65m, an increase of £1.15m above the £4.5m approved budget.
findings.detail: Unforeseen ground conditions and site history have driven additional costs. The contractor's bid was £3.2m based on neutral ground assumptions; the approved budget of £4.5m was intended to provide contingency. Construction has been delayed by soft ground requiring excavation and replacement, drainage diversions, a high-voltage cable diversion, and geotechnical concerns, with the site now expected to remain closed until early 2027.
findings.matters: Material capital budget increase of 26% above approved amount requires GMCA approval and extends the funding requirement; a lender needs to understand the scale of the overrun and funding source.
findings.figures: £4.5m approved budget, £3.2m contractor bid, £5.65m forecast, £1.15m increase, site reopening moved to early 2027
findings.quote: Due to the number and complexity of additional works the overall budget is now forecasted at £5.65m.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Waste & Recycling Committee
findings.headline: Materials recovery facility planning application delayed by 9 months; procurement paused for 6 months pending planning approval.
findings.detail: The MRF planning application submitted in January 2026 remains unresolved as of September 2026, delayed by environmental, traffic and noise concerns; Bolton Council raised additional noise concerns in June following a 60-home development within 200m of the site. Noise modelling identified glass handling as a risk, leading to a proposed 20m x 25m rear extension to contain it indoors. The procurement process has been paused for six months pending planning approval, with preferred supplier appointment forecast for January 2027 and completion expected summer 2028.
findings.matters: Planning delays in capital projects create uncertainty about delivery timelines and may expose councils to cost inflation and extended interim arrangements; six-month procurement pause indicates material timeline risk.
findings.figures: Planning application submitted January 2026; decision expected October 2026. Procurement paused 6 months. Preferred supplier forecast January 2027. Completion expected summer 2028.
findings.quote: As a result of these delays the procurement process is now paused for six months and will restart once planning is secured.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Waste & Recycling Committee
findings.headline: Northern slope stability issue on HWRC site requires retaining wall at estimated cost of £700–850k with 15-week programme.
findings.detail: A slope stability assessment identified settlement risk along the northern slope due to its steep gradient and poor-quality made ground. The solution is a piled retaining wall with 75 concrete piles installed to 18 metres below ground level, estimated at £700–850k with a 15-week programme, though both figures remain subject to further design review.
findings.matters: Geotechnical risks in capital projects can trigger further cost growth and programme slippage; this identifies a major cost element still under review.
findings.figures: 75 concrete piles; 18m below ground level; estimated 15-week programme; £700–850k estimated cost (both tbc).
findings.quote: A slope stability assessment has identified a settlement risk along the northern slope due to its steep gradient and poor-quality made ground. A retaining structure is therefore required to stabilise the slope and surrounding area.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Waste & Recycling Committee
findings.headline: Capital budget for household waste recycling centre rebuild increased from £4.5m to £5.65m due to site conditions discovered during construction.
findings.detail: The HWRC capital budget has been increased by £1.15m to £5.65m. Key cost drivers include unknown historic piles from a former anaerobic digestion plant, extensive drainage diversions, poor made ground requiring additional excavation, HV cable diversion, and geotechnical stability concerns on the northern slope. Construction began in September 2025 and as of 10 September 2026, site clearance, demolition, remediation, piling and drainage works are progressing.
findings.matters: Material budget increases in capital schemes signal delivery risks and may indicate further cost exposure; councils and lenders need visibility of revised project economics.
findings.figures: Original budget £4.5m, revised to £5.65m (increase of £1.15m). Northern slope retaining wall estimated at £700–850k for 75 concrete piles at 18m depth with 15-week programme (both TBC).
findings.quote: Costs impact – Increased capital budget form £4.5m to £5.65m

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Combined Authority Audit Committee
findings.headline: Bank Rate to remain at 3.75% through 2026, falling to 3.25% by spring 2028
findings.detail: Monetary Policy Committee held Bank Rate at 3.75% at both Q1 meetings (30 April and 18 June 2026). MUFG treasury advisors forecast rates to remain on hold through 2026, with next reductions beginning H2 2027, reaching 3.25% by spring 2028, contingent on Consumer Price Index inflation peaking around 3.6%.
findings.matters: Interest rate forecast directly affects GMCA's refinancing strategy and future borrowing costs; peer councils rely on this context for their own borrowing decisions and market timing.
findings.figures: Bank Rate held at 3.75%; PWLB rates at 30 June 2026: 1-year 4.77%, 5-year 5.07%, 10-year 5.55%, 25-year 6.17%; forecast Bank Rate 3.5% by end 2027, 3.25% by spring 2028
findings.quote: We forecast the next reduction in Bank Rate to be made in H2 2027, with Bank Rate falling to a low of 3.25% by the start of 2028.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Combined Authority Audit Committee
findings.headline: Authority achieved 4.04% average investment yield, outperforming SONIA by 31 basis points, on track for £9.67m budgeted return
findings.detail: With average funds of £473.7m invested across banks, councils, and money market funds, the authority exceeded Sterling Overnight Index Average returns through active treasury management. Budgeted investment return for 2026/27 of £9.67m is currently forecast to be achieved.
findings.matters: Investment income is material cash generator for the authority; outperformance against SONIA demonstrates effective treasury management and supports cash position.
findings.figures: Average investment rate 4.04% versus SONIA 3.73%; outperformance 0.31bps; budgeted return £9.670m; average funds invested £473.7m
findings.quote: The Authority achieved an average rate of 4.04% which outperformed the average backward looking Sterling Overnight Index Average (SONIA) rate by 0.31 bps. The Authority's budgeted investment return for 2026/27 is £9.670m, and we are currently forecast to achieve this.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Combined Authority Audit Committee
findings.headline: Gross external debt forecast at £1,574.4m, £182.9m below budget; net borrowing declining
findings.detail: Both gross external debt and net borrowing are declining from budgeted levels. Gross debt forecast at £1,574.4m versus budget of £1,757.3m, and net borrowing at £1,518.4m versus budget of £1,707.3m. Ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream improving to 6.9% from budgeted 7.6%.
findings.matters: Falling debt across the balance sheet improves credit metrics and reduces refinancing volumes, positive signal to lenders on credit trajectory and debt serviceability.
findings.figures: Gross external debt £1,574.381m (budget £1,757.263m); Net borrowing £1,518.381m (budget £1,707.263m); Ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream 6.9% (budget 7.6%)
findings.quote: Gross external debt as at 31 March £1,757.263m £1,574.381m; Net borrowing as at 31 March £1,707.263m £1,518.381m

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Combined Authority Audit Committee
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement forecast at £2,688.3m, £305.7m below budget
findings.detail: The Capital Financing Requirement is forecast to fall from budgeted £2,994.0m to £2,688.3m, with annual change in CFR £182.3m against budgeted £453.3m, and in-year borrowing requirement £370.0m against budgeted £567.0m. The paper does not explain whether this represents slippage in capital delivery, deferral of planned projects, or efficiency improvements.
findings.matters: A 10% reduction in planned capital investment affects both immediate borrowing need and the multi-year capital programme outlook; peer councils monitoring how others manage capital programmes in the current market, and lenders assessing whether deferral indicates financial constraint or prudent timing.
findings.figures: Capital expenditure £994.747m (budget £1,148.913m); Capital Financing Requirement £2,688.288m (budget £2,994.019m); Annual change in CFR £182.271m (budget £453.281m); In year borrowing requirement £370.000m (budget £566.956m)
findings.quote: Prudential Indicators 2025/26 Budget 2026/27 Forecast Capital expenditure £1,148.913m £994.747m Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) £2,994.019m £2,688.288m

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Police, Fire and Crime Panel
findings.headline: PCC grant funding expected to increase for violence reduction, victims services, youth justice and domestic abuse perpetrator intervention pending formal confirmation and Home Office bid outcomes due October 2026
findings.detail: Supplies and services spend increased to £5.4m following confirmation of awards. Additionally, MoJ grant for Youth Justice Services (Turnaround) of £1m and proposal for Domestic Abuse Perpetrator Intervention funding extension of £0.3m are pending. Six further Home Office bids totalling £2.331m have been submitted with outcomes due in October 2026.
findings.matters: Grant income volatility and pending confirmations mean PCC's outturn is not certain. Failed bids or withdrawn funding would require alternate funding or additional reserve draws.
findings.figures: £1m (Youth Justice); £0.3m (Domestic Abuse); £2.331m (six Home Office bids pending)
findings.quote: Grant income and corresponding expenditure is expected to increase for 2026/27 pending formal confirmation. This includes an MoJ grant award for Youth Justice Services (Turnaround) of £1m and a proposal to extend the Domestic Abuse Perpetrator Intervention Funding for 3 months for £0.3m.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Police, Fire and Crime Panel
findings.headline: Police & Crime Commissioner running costs forecast at £38.3m against budget of £36.4m, variance of £1.9m (5%), being balanced by additional reserve draws beyond budget
findings.detail: PCC supplies and services spend increased from £2.5m to £5.4m following confirmation of grant awards for Violence Reduction Unit and Victims Services. This drove running costs variance to £1.9m, which PCC is offsetting through additional reserve draws of £1.9m (160% variance against budgeted £1.2m draw).
findings.matters: PCC running costs overspend is being masked by larger reserve draws rather than being recovered through other measures, increasing overall reserve depletion for the combined authority.
findings.figures: £38.3m forecast vs £36.4m budget; £1.9m variance (5%)
findings.quote: Running Costs 36,427 (budget) 38,342 (forecast) 1,915 (variance)

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Police, Fire and Crime Panel
findings.headline: Greater Manchester Police starting strength 3,459.09 FTE against budget of 3,450 FTE, creating pressure equivalent to £0.45m for 9 FTE above plan, being managed through strict vacancy control
findings.detail: Final 2025/26 strength and therefore 2026/27 opening strength was 3,459.09 FTE, exceeding budget of 3,450 FTE. Paper notes "The impact of every 10 staff over the budgeted strength equates to £0.5m in a full financial year", meaning current overage of 9 FTE creates approximately £0.45m pressure. GMP implementing "significant scrutiny of all Police staff vacancies" and "strict vacancy management" to bring strength back to budget.
findings.matters: Staff strength above establishment creates ongoing payroll pressure. Recruitment controls are discretionary tools and success in reducing strength back to budget is uncertain.
findings.figures: 3,459.09 FTE actual vs 3,450 FTE budget; £0.5m per 10 FTE per annum
findings.quote: The final strength for 2025/26 and therefore the starting strength for 2026/27 was 3,459.09 FTE which is slightly above the budgeted start point.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Police, Fire and Crime Panel
findings.headline: Unbudgeted costs of £0.320m quantified for June 2026 moorland fires with further costs emerging for pay, equipment replacement and recovery, subject to Bellwin criteria recovery
findings.detail: GMFRS declared a Major Incident for moorland fires in June 2026. Quantified spend to date is £0.320m, but further costs are anticipated for pay, replacement equipment, and recovery operations. Authority will monitor spend against Bellwin criteria and seek cost recovery through those guidelines.
findings.matters: Emergency incidents create unbudgeted cost pressures. Extent of further costs is uncertain, and recovery will depend on Bellwin eligibility and Home Office approval; costs may become permanent if not recoverable.
findings.figures: £0.320m quantified to date; further costs unknown
findings.quote: Following the recent Major Incident declared in relation to the Moorland Fires, unbudgeted costs of £0.320m has been quantified as spend to date with known information, however, there will be further pay costs, replacement equipment, and recovery costs.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Police, Fire and Crime Panel
findings.headline: Greater Manchester Fire & Rescue Service capital programme forecast at £28.1m against £44.4m budget, representing £16.3m slippage (37%) primarily from estates and vehicle procurement delays
findings.detail: Capital underspend driven by: Estates £8m (Heywood and Withington new builds reprofiled to 2027/28), Transport £5.4m (12 operational vehicles delayed to 2027/28), Equipment £3.4m. Completed projects include Blackley (opened July 2026) with Whitefield and Stockport expected to finish September 2026. Phase 1 of long-term estates strategy is underway with £13m additional funding from Deputy Mayor.
findings.matters: Major capital programme delays indicate timeline slippage and potential knock-on effects for asset replacement and service resilience. However, completion of Blackley suggests programme is progressing despite delays.
findings.figures: £28.1m forecast vs £44.4m budget; £16.3m variance (37%)
findings.quote: The movement from budget relates to reprofiling of the Heywood and Withington New Builds, with the majority of spend originally planned for the current year but now expected in 2027/28.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Police, Fire and Crime Panel
findings.headline: Greater Manchester Fire & Rescue Service achieving balanced Q1 2026/27 position, with pay awards cheaper than budget and pension opt-outs offsetting operational pressures
findings.detail: GMFRS forecast outturn of £160.7m matches budget of £160.4m, a variance of just £0.3m (0%). Breakeven is achieved after reserve transfers of £2.1m in and £1.6m out. Firefighter pay award of 3.8% came in £0.077m cheaper than assumed 4%; Green Book award of 3.3% created £0.048m pressure. A £3.26m underspend on employer pension contributions results from 145 staff opting out of pension scheme.
findings.matters: GMFRS has maintained budget control while managing unbudgeted moorland fire costs and staffing changes, providing a counterbalance to GMP's deteriorating position.
findings.figures: £160.7m forecast vs £160.4m budget; £0.3m variance (0%); £3.26m pension opt-out saving; £0.077m pay award saving
findings.quote: The overall Quarter 1 forecast indicates a breakeven position after reserve movements.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Police, Fire and Crime Panel
findings.headline: Combined authority forecast to call on reserves by £8.5m in 2026/27, 47% higher than budgeted £4.6m, representing material increase in reserve depletion
findings.detail: Budgeted reserve draws of £4.6m are now forecast at £8.5m. This comprises GMFRS drawing £1.6m (planned capital transfers), GMP drawing £3.8m (10% variance), and PCC drawing additional £1.9m (160% variance against budget of £1.2m). Growing calls on reserves indicate services are not balanced within approved budgets.
findings.matters: Increasing reliance on reserves to balance budgets is unsustainable. Reserve balances are finite and one-off funding sources; persistent use signals ongoing structural imbalance that will require future budget action.
findings.figures: £4.6m budgeted; £8.5m forecast; £2.7m additional draw (47% increase)
findings.quote: Reserves -4,631 (Base Budget 2026/27) -5,786 (Current Budget 2026/27) -8,500 (Forecast)

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Police, Fire and Crime Panel
findings.headline: Greater Manchester Police submitting bid to Home Office for Exceptional Financial Support in response to recurring £9.8m budget challenge
findings.detail: Home Office launched a financial Resilience Framework allowing forces and local policing bodies to bid for Exceptional Financial Support. GMP is compiling a bid to be submitted in September 2026. The paper explicitly acknowledges "recurring financial challenges that GMP has faced over a number of years" as the context for the submission.
findings.matters: An application for emergency government support signals the force cannot solve its budget gap through internal measures alone. The bid outcome will determine whether GMP must identify further savings, service reductions, or draw additional reserves if unsuccessful.
findings.figures: £9.8m is the budget gap being addressed by the bid
findings.quote: Given the recurring financial challenges that GMP has faced over a number of years and the current position set out here, a bid is currently being compiled and will be submitted later this month.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Police, Fire and Crime Panel
findings.headline: Police officer overtime forecast at £24.1m against budget of £18.8m, representing 28% variance driven by operational demand despite prior control mechanisms
findings.detail: Overtime is identified as "one of the biggest risk areas on the Force budget". The base budget was not increased for 2026/27 due to overall financial pressures. Within four months of the year, the paper states "a significant overspend is likely in 2026/27 and given the operational demand pressures is likely to increase further", indicating this pressure will worsen as the year progresses.
findings.matters: Overtime is the single largest driver of GMP's £9.8m deficit. If this continues to worsen, it will materially impact year-end outturn and the authority's ability to balance without external intervention.
findings.figures: £24.1m forecast; £18.8m budget; £5.2m variance (28%)
findings.quote: It is evident after just a few months that a significant overspend is likely in 2026/27 and given the operational demand pressures is likely to increase further.

findings.committee: Greater Manchester Police, Fire and Crime Panel
findings.headline: Greater Manchester Police forecasting £9.8m overspend against approved opening budget of £875.9m based on July position after four months
findings.detail: Full year forecast outturn at £885.7m compared to approved opening budget of £875.9m. Main drivers are overtime costs (£5.2m overspend on £18.8m budget), base pay costs (£4.3m overspend), and pension costs (£1.4m overspend). The forecast is based on only four months of data and acknowledges it is subject to change, but the paper states the position is "likely to worsen" given operational demand pressures.
findings.matters: A £9.8m overspend on a £876m budget signals material uncontrolled cost growth and raises questions about whether GMP can deliver within its approved financial envelope without external support.
findings.figures: £9.8m overspend; £875.9m opening budget; £885.7m forecast outturn
findings.quote: The full year forecast position as at the end of July 2026 shows an overspend of £9.8m against the approved opening budget of £875.9m.

findings.detail: All 11 grant certifications in 2025/26 received positive assurance, covering £72.055m, confirming compliant spend on Local Energy Advice Demonstrators, Growth Hub, SHDF, 5G Innovations, Brownfield Housing Fund, Net Zero programmes and Made Smarter grants.
